hook.core: A video with **2 million likes** says a herbal tea **cured** someone's anxiety in three days. The comments say *“This worked for me too!”* There's a discount code in the bio. Another video says it's rubbish. Who do you believe? And who could you actually ask?

why.support: Some health info online is true. Some isn't. Learn to check **who** made it and what **proof** it has. Learn to ask clear questions. Then you can look after your own health.
why.core: Health information is everywhere, but not all of it is true. Some is made by experts. Some is made by people selling something. Learning to check **who** made it, what **evidence** it has, and how **careful** its words are helps you find information you can trust. And knowing how to ask a doctor or pharmacist clear questions means you get the right answers about your own health.
why.extend: Health information circulates through texts with very different purposes: public health guidance, personal stories and marketing. Evaluating source, evidence and language (especially the difference between careful, qualified claims and absolute ones) lets you judge reliability. Clear spoken questions, and checking you've understood, let you take part in your own health care.

articles.title: Health info you can trust

body.support:
Health info is everywhere online. Some is true. Some is wrong. Some is selling something.

**1. Who made it?** A doctor or a health website? Or someone selling something?

**2. What's the proof?** *“It worked for me!”* is a story, not **evidence**. Likes aren't proof.

**3. Watch the words.** Good health info says **may** or **can**. Be careful of *cure*, *miracle* or *100%*.

**4. Check a trusted site.** Try **healthdirect** or **headspace**.

**5. Ask a professional.** A doctor, **pharmacist** or school nurse can help. **headspace** helps 12 to 25 year olds, for free or a low cost. In an emergency, call **000**.

**Ask clear questions.** Write them down first. Then say the answer back: *So I take it twice a day?*

**Privacy.** What you tell a doctor is usually **confidential** (private).
body.core:
Health information is everywhere: on TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and from friends. Some of it is great. Some is wrong, and some is trying to sell you something. Here's how to tell the difference.

**1. Who made it?** Was it a **health professional** or a health organisation, like a hospital or a government health website? Or someone sharing their story? Or someone **selling** something? Check their name, their training, and whether there's a product or discount code.

**2. What's the evidence?** Reliable health information explains **why** it's true, and often links to research. A personal story, *“It worked for me!”*, is not **evidence**. Neither are likes, views or comments.

**3. Watch the words.** Careful health information uses words like **may**, **can**, **might** and **for some people**, because bodies are different. Be wary of big **claims**: *cure*, *miracle*, *100%*, *guaranteed*, or *doctors don't want you to know this*.

**4. Check it somewhere you trust.** Compare it with **healthdirect**, the **Better Health Channel** (from the Victorian Government) or **headspace**. If they say something different, trust them.

**5. Ask a professional.** A GP, **pharmacist** or school nurse can help. **headspace** offers free or low-cost support for 12 to 25 year olds. The **healthdirect** helpline (1800 022 222) lets you talk to a nurse, for free, 24 hours a day. In an emergency, call **000**.

**Asking clear questions.** Before an appointment, write down what's been happening, when it started, and your questions. During it, say the answer back to check: *So I take it twice a day, with food?* And ask: *What should I do if it doesn't get better?*

**Your privacy.** What you tell a doctor is usually **confidential**. They may have to share it if someone could be seriously harmed. Once you're **14**, your parents can't see your Medicare claims online unless you agree. At **15**, you can get your own Medicare card.
body.extend:
Young people encounter health information constantly, through social media, video platforms and peers. Its reliability varies widely, so evaluating it is a core health skill.

**1. Identify the source and purpose.** Is it from a **health professional** or health organisation (a hospital, a government health service)? A personal account? A business? Check credentials and look for commercial motives such as products, affiliate links or discount codes.

**2. Assess the evidence.** Reliable sources explain their reasoning and cite research. **Testimonials** (*“It worked for me!”*), likes and comments are not **evidence**, however persuasive they feel.

**3. Read the language.** Reliable health writing is **qualified**: *may*, *can*, *some people*, *evidence suggests*. This reflects real variation between people. Absolute **claims** (*cure*, *miracle*, *100%*, *guaranteed*) and appeals to suspicion (*doctors don't want you to know*) are warning signs.

**4. Compare with authoritative sources** such as **healthdirect**, the Victorian Government's **Better Health Channel** or **headspace**.

**5. Consult a professional.** GPs, **pharmacists** and school nurses can help. **headspace** provides free or low-cost support for 12 to 25 year olds, and the free **healthdirect** helpline (1800 022 222) connects you with a registered nurse 24/7. In an emergency, call **000**.

**Communicating clearly.** Prepare a short history (what, when, what helps or worsens it) and your questions. Paraphrase advice back to confirm it, and ask what to do if things don't improve.

**Privacy.** Consultations are usually **confidential**, with exceptions where someone faces serious harm. From **14**, parents can't view your Medicare claims online without your consent, and from **15** you can hold your own Medicare card.

caseStudies.title: Where teens get health advice

body.support:
The **Royal Children's Hospital** in Melbourne asked **1,488 teens** about health info. That was in **2025**.

What it found:

- **63%** of teens get health info from **social media**.
- Only **27%** would go to social media to **look** for it.

So most teens see health info without looking for it. It just pops up.

That's why it's important to check **who** made it.
body.core:
The **Royal Children's Hospital** in Melbourne runs a **National Child Health Poll**. In **August 2025**, it shared a poll about teens, health and social media. It asked **1,488 Australian teens** aged 12 to 17, and their parents.

Here's what it found:

- **63%** of teens said they get health information from **social media**.
- But only **27%** said they would turn to social media if they were **looking** for health information on purpose.

So most teens are seeing health messages on social media **without even looking for them**. They pop up in their feeds, between videos about sport, music and friends.

That matters. Information you didn't look for can still shape what you believe. Check **who** made it, and what **evidence** it has. That's how you know if it's worth believing.
body.extend:
The **Royal Children's Hospital** in Melbourne runs the **National Child Health Poll**. Its **August 2025** poll surveyed **1,488 Australian teenagers** aged 12 to 17, and their parents, about health messages and social media.

- **63%** of teens said they get health information from **social media**.
- Only **27%** said they would turn to social media if they were **deliberately** looking for health information.

The gap suggests most exposure is **passive**. Health content arrives in feeds whether teens are looking for it or not. Its source and purpose often aren't clear.

Passive exposure still shapes beliefs. So the skills you'd use when researching (checking the source, evidence and language) matter just as much when you're scrolling.

caseStudies.title: Who made the video?

body.support:
A team at **La Trobe**, a uni in Melbourne, looked at **100 TikTok videos** about birth control. The videos were very popular.

What they found:

- Only **10%** were made by doctors or nurses.
- Most were people's own stories.
- Some were from influencers.

The top video is not always right. Check **who** made it.
body.core:
Researchers at **La Trobe University** studied **100 popular TikTok videos** about birth control. Together, they had nearly **five billion views**. The study came out in **2025**.

Here's what they found:

- Only **10%** of the videos were made by **health professionals**.
- **53%** of the creators clearly rejected hormonal birth control.
- About a **third** said they didn't trust health professionals.

Most videos were personal stories, or advice from wellness influencers. The researchers warned that videos about bad experiences get more attention. So the app shows them to more people.

The lesson isn't about one topic. On any health question, the most popular video may not be made by someone who knows the most. Check **who** made it.
body.extend:
Researchers at **La Trobe University** analysed **100 popular TikTok videos** about contraception. Together, they had nearly **five billion views**. The peer-reviewed study was published in **2025**.

- Only **10%** of the videos were made by **health professionals**.
- **53%** of creators clearly rejected hormonal contraception.
- About a **third** said they distrusted health professionals.

Most videos were personal stories or advice from wellness influencers. The researchers noted that apps tend to promote bad experiences, because those videos get more engagement.

The finding goes beyond this topic. Popularity and expertise are different things. When an algorithm, not an editor, decides what you see, you need to check who made a text, and why.

teacher.overview: Students learn to evaluate health information: who made it and why, what evidence it offers, and how careful its language is (qualified claims with *may*, *can* and *some people* versus absolute claims like *cure* and *100%*). They compare claims with authoritative sources (healthdirect, the Better Health Channel, headspace), learn where young people can get help, and practise asking clear questions and paraphrasing advice in a role-played appointment. Case studies: the RCH National Child Health Poll (2025) on teens and social media, and La Trobe University's 2025 study of popular TikTok birth control videos.
prep: Make simple GP or pharmacist role-play cards (e.g. *a sprained ankle: rest, ice, see a physio if no better in a week*). Keep advice general and safe.
Check healthdirect, the Better Health Channel and headspace are reachable on school devices.
Let your wellbeing team know you're teaching this, in case it prompts students to seek help.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** who made it (and why)? What's the evidence? Are the words careful? Does a trusted source agree? Likes and comments show popularity, not whether it's true. Help: GP, pharmacist, school nurse, headspace, healthdirect.

**Post:** 1 creator (no qualifications); 2 big claim (cured, 100%); 3 distrust of doctors; 4 not evidence (stories, likes); 5 selling (discount code); 6 missing (sources, date, side effects).

**Sort:** healthdirect — trust; influencer selling — check; 3 million likes — check; pharmacist — trust; 100% guaranteed — check; Better Health Channel — trust.

**Careful or big? (samples):** exercise can help — careful; acne cream — big (*may help some people's skin over several weeks*); 4 litres — big (*how much water you need depends on your body and activity*); more sleep — careful.

**Case studies:** 63% get health information from social media, but only 27% would look for it there, so most exposure is passive; messages you didn't seek can still shape beliefs. Only 10% of the videos were made by health professionals, so popular isn't the same as accurate.

realityCheck: **Health is personal.** Never ask students to share real health problems. The plan and role-play work with made-up problems.
**The La Trobe case is about birth control.** It's left out of the support level. Check it fits your school's health and sexuality education approach before teaching it.
**Some students will need help.** Have headspace, Kids Helpline and your school's wellbeing contacts ready, and tell students where to find them.
**Confidentiality has limits.** Be clear that doctors keep things private except where someone could be seriously harmed. Your school's own rules for teachers may differ.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students already scroll health content daily; this gives them tools to question it.
